chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'adah ibn Sadah, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: He was asked about that which is not permissible regarding intention by implicit reference (israr) in an oath, so he said: 'It is permissible in one case and not permissible in another. As for that which is permissible: if the swearer is the one wronged (mazlum), then what he swore by and intended the oath for is according to his own intention. And as for if he is the one doing the wronging (zhalim), then the oath is according to the intention of the wronged one.'
ai.seo_question: How does the status of the swearer (oppressor or oppressed) affect the validity of an oath with implicit intention in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between the victim (mazlum) and the oppressor (zhalim) regarding oaths with implicit intention (israr), ruling that the victim's intent prevails in both cases to ensure fairness. This principle reflects the Shia juristic emphasis on protecting the weaker party from the ambiguity of the swearer's hidden thoughts, ensuring the oath aligns with justice rather than potential deceit.
